persona.name: Anjali
persona.profile: Seven years of C#/.NET in enterprise logistics; has done domain modelling workshops and thinks in aggregates, value objects and policies. Tends toward more classes rather than fewer, each small and named from the business language. Documents assumptions and trade-offs at length because her reviews get read by people who were not in the room.

assumptions: Cash payment is handled at exit gate by a Cashier service.
Vehicle size hierarchy: Motorcycle fits Small, Car fits Medium, Truck fits Large.
Spot size hierarchy: Small, Medium, Large; larger spots can host smaller vehicles if no exact match.
Ticket is a value object containing entry time and assigned spot.

design.tradeoffs: More classes increase expressive power and align with domain language, but add boilerplate; chosen to keep each concept explicit for future extensibility.

decisions.what: Use Spot.CanFit to allow larger spots to host smaller vehicles
decisions.why: Reflects real parking lots where a car can use a large spot if no medium is free, improving utilization without extra complexity.

decisions.what: Represent Ticket as immutable value object
decisions.why: Simplifies reasoning about fee calculation and audit; tickets never change after issuance.

decisions.why: Separates concerns, makes fee policy replaceable (e.g., future credit card integration).

designReport:
Report for the design stage (overall so far 2):
- requirement-coverage: 3/4 — 1 of 6 requirements have nothing in the design that speaks to them: "Entry is refused when no suitable spot is free". Suggestion: Add a class that owns each missing requirement, or state in your assumptions why it is out of scope.
- class-responsibilities: 0/4 — Cashier lists 3 separate responsibilities in one sentence: "Calculates fee based on vehicle type and duration, receives cash.". ParkingLot lists 3 separate responsibilities in one sentence: "Manages floors and coordinates entry and exit operations.". Vehicle lists 3 separate responsibilities in one sentence: "Base type for all vehicles, provides size and rate information.". Suggestion: Split Cashier. Pull out the responsibility with the fewest dependencies on the rest — usually calculation rather than coordination.
- coupling-cohesion: 2/4 — VehicleType, Ticket are declared but connected to nothing — usually a noun taken from the brief before deciding what it does. Suggestion: Either connect each orphan to the classes that use it, or drop it.
- abstraction-use: 2/4 — spot allocation strategy has no seam in the design at all, and nearest-to-entrance, floor-fill, and reserved-first are all legitimate and swappable. Suggestion: Introduce an interface for spot allocation strategy and move the varying behaviour behind it.
- behaviour: 2/4 — Step 4 of "A car arrives and parks" calls Ticket.<ctor>, but Ticket does not declare a method called <ctor>. The walkthrough and the class disagree about what Ticket can do. "A car leaves and pays" never touches anything pricing- or rate-shaped, so it is not clear where that part of the work happens. Suggestion: Either add the method to the class or move the step to the class that really owns it — the mismatch is telling you which.
- edge-cases: 3/4 — The refusal path is only described informally (null or an undocumented exception) and not represented by a concrete domain type in the model. Suggestion: Introduce an explicit result type (e.g., EntryResult enum or a dedicated EntryRefused exception class) that the caller must handle, removing reliance on null returns.

assumptions: Cash payment is handled at exit gate by a PaymentProcessor service.
Vehicle size hierarchy: Motorcycle fits Small, Car fits Medium, Truck fits Large.
Spot size hierarchy: Small, Medium, Large; larger spots can host smaller vehicles if no exact match.
Ticket is an immutable value object containing entry time, spot id and optional charging session id.
Electric vehicles may be assigned to a ChargingSpot which records kWh consumed.

revisedDesign.tradeoffs: More classes (FeeCalculator, PaymentProcessor, AllocationStrategy) increase separation of concerns and make pricing or allocation policies swappable; added ChargingSpot and related attributes to support kWh billing without disturbing time‑based flow.

decisions.why: Creates a seam for future strategies (nearest, floor‑fill, reserved) and satisfies abstraction‑use feedback.

decisions.what: Split Cashier into FeeCalculator and PaymentProcessor
decisions.alternative: Single Cashier class handling both pricing and cash collection
decisions.why: Reduces a single class having multiple responsibilities; aligns with SRP and the coupling‑cohesion comment.

decisions.alternative: Treat charging as a separate service unrelated to Spot
decisions.why: Charging is fundamentally a kind of Spot with extra state; keeping it in the aggregate avoids orphaned classes.
Makes the refusal path explicit, eliminates reliance on null and satisfies edge‑case feedback.

decisions.what: Make Ticket immutable and include optional charging session
decisions.why: Preserves auditability; a Ticket never changes after issuance, even for electric sessions.

rationale: I added a ChargingSpot subclass and extended Ticket to capture a charging session so we can bill kWh instead of time; split the monolithic Cashier into FeeCalculator (pure pricing) and PaymentProcessor (cash handling) to give each class a single responsibility; introduced ISpotAllocationStrategy with a concrete NearestEntranceStrategy to expose allocation seams; made refusal explicit via EntryResult and EntryRefusedException; wired the new types into the existing aggregates and updated relationships to use only the allowed kinds.
changeReport:
Report for the change stage (overall so far 2.1):
- change-resilience: 3/4 — Added ChargingSpot, ElectricCar, FeeCalculator, PaymentProcessor, ISpotAllocationStrategy, NearestEntranceStrategy, EntryResult, EntryRefusedException, ExitRequest behind Vehicle, which already existed. 5 existing classes were reopened: ParkingLot (responsibility, attributes, methods); Floor (responsibility); Spot (responsibility); Vehicle (responsibility, methods); Ticket (responsibility, attributes). Cashier was removed. If that was a rename, the rationale should say so — the evaluator cannot tell a rename from a replacement. Suggestion: Reduce the wiring: only one existing class should need to know ChargingSpot exists.

Mentor's note: The most impactful change would be to reduce how many existing classes depend on the new ChargingSpot. In the current design, several classes – ParkingLot, Floor, Spot, Ticket – all reference ChargingSpot, creating tight coupling. Because charging is a specialized kind of spot, you can keep the ChargingSpot type but have only ParkingLot handle the creation and wiring of charging sessions. Move the charging‐specific responsibilities (start/stop, kWh tracking) into the ParkingLot’s exit process and let Spot remain unaware of charging, while Ticket can simply hold a chargingSessionId without needing to know the concrete spot type. First, refactor ParkingLot so that it is the sole class that knows about ChargingSpot and delegates all charging logic to it, and remove direct ChargingSpot references from Floor, Spot and Ticket. This will simplify the object model and make future extensions easier.

p-split.text: Cashier describes more than one job. If you had to split it into two classes tonight, where is the cut — and which of the two does Ticket talk to?

We split the “Cashier” along the SRP boundary: **FeeCalculator** owns all pricing rules (time‑based rates, kWh tariffs, discounts, etc.) and is completely pure; **PaymentProcessor** owns the transactional side (accepting cash, cards, issuing receipts, updating the spot state).  

Ticket never calls either – it’s a pure value object. At exit the **PaymentProcessor** receives an ExitRequest that contains the Ticket, extracts the needed data and then delegates the fee‑computation to FeeCalculator. In other words, Ticket is handed to the PaymentProcessor, which in turn uses the FeeCalculator.
Why does the Ticket class not invoke the FeeCalculator to compute the exit fee instead of delegating through the PaymentProcessor?

Ticket is a pure value object – it only captures immutable facts (spot id, entry time, optional session id). Computing a fee is a domain policy, not intrinsic data. Keeping Ticket free of behavior preserves its auditability and lets us reuse it in other contexts (e.g., reporting, dispute resolution) without pulling in pricing logic. PaymentProcessor is the application service that orchestrates the exit use‑case; it knows the request shape and can coordinate side‑effects (payment, spot release). It therefore passes the Ticket to FeeCalculator, which remains a stateless policy component. This separation also makes unit‑testing easier: we can test FeeCalculator in isolation and mock PaymentProcessor’s transactional concerns.

p-pricing.text: Weekend rates start next month. Which method in your design changes, and which other classes have to know about it?

The only place that actually encodes the pricing policy is **FeeCalculator.CalculateFee** – that’s where we look at the vehicle’s hourly rate and apply any modifiers. To support a weekend‑rate we’d add a “date / day‑of‑week” parameter (or inject a IDateProvider) and adjust the calculation logic there.

Because **PaymentProcessor.ProcessPayment** delegates straight to FeeCalculator, it needs to supply the extra date information (or the injected provider). If we go the provider route, the provider itself becomes a new dependency of both PaymentProcessor (and potentially any other service that needs to know “is it weekend?” – e.g. a reporting module). No other domain classes (Vehicle, Spot, etc.) need to change because the weekend rule lives entirely in the pricing policy component.
Does your Ticket class need to store the entry date so that FeeCalculator can apply the weekend rate, and if so, how will that affect Ticket creation?

Ticket already carries the entry DateTime (named entryTime). That’s exactly the timestamp we need to decide whether the stay crossed a weekend period. No change to the Ticket shape is required; we just keep the existing immutable constructor and pass the same entryTime when we create it in Spot.Assign (or ChargingSpot.StartCharging).  

If we wanted the fee to be based on “weekend‑only” rates (e.g., a flat weekend multiplier regardless of the day of exit), we could still compute it from the stored entryTime and the exit timestamp supplied in ExitRequest. The only impact is that ExitVehicle must ensure the ExitRequest includes the exit DateTime so FeeCalculator.CalculateFee has both boundaries; Ticket itself stays untouched.

p-refusal.text: A motorcycle arrives and every motorcycle spot is taken. Which class says no, and what exactly does the caller receive — a null, an exception, a result type?

The refusal is raised by **ParkingLot.EnterVehicle**. Inside it we call **Floor.FindSpotFor**, which delegates to the configured **ISpotAllocationStrategy**. If the strategy cannot pick a spot it returns null, and **ParkingLot** translates that into an **EntryRefusedException** (or, if you prefer the enum path, it returns EntryResult.Refused). In the current design the public contract is the exception – callers catch EntryRefusedException and inspect its Reason property. The enum is only there for internal use or for callers that explicitly ask for a result‑type flow.
When ParkingLot throws an EntryRefusedException, does it still create a Ticket object, or does it skip ticket creation entirely?

No – the ticket is only created after we have a concrete Spot to assign. ParkingLot.EnterVehicle first asks the Floor (and ultimately the ISpotAllocationStrategy) for a spot. If the strategy returns null we raise EntryRefusedException *before* any call to Spot.Assign or Ticket construction. So the exception short‑circuits the flow; no Ticket instance is emitted, and the caller gets only the exception (or, alternatively, an EntryResult.Refused if they use the enum‑only path). This keeps the audit log clean – we never persist a ticket for a vehicle that never entered.

defendReport:
Report for the defend stage (overall so far 2.1):

Mentor's note: The most impactful improvement is adding a concrete alternative scenario for the FeeCalculator/PaymentProcessor split, such as a very small lot where a single Cashier class would suffice; this shows you can revert the split when complexity is low and explains when the abstraction is overkill. Explain why the separation matters for larger lots (multiple rates, multi‑currency), and then, first, document that scenario and note when you would merge the classes into one for simplicity.

exit.q1: Yes – the coupling‑resilience note that I had introduced ChargingSpot into four existing aggregates was new to me; I hadn’t realized how much ripple that would cause across the model, so the mentor’s suggestion to centralise the knowledge in ParkingLot was an eye‑opener.
exit.q2: I initially thought the "class-responsibilities" criterion was over‑critical; I argued that a sentence listing several duties was acceptable as long as the responsibilities were cohesive, but the feedback correctly flagged that each aggregate should own a single, well‑named responsibility to keep the model clean.
exit.q3: I would definitely share this exercise because it highlights concrete pitfalls – orphan types, hidden seams, and over‑coupling of new domain concepts – that are easy to miss in a timed interview, and it shows how to document trade‑offs and refactor iteratively, which are valuable interview skills.
